identity.title: Real-Time Hyper-Personalized Generative AI Should Be Regulated to Prevent the Rise of "Digital Heroin"

problem.claim: The paper addresses the risk that real-time, hyper-personalized generative AI could create addictive digital content, especially harming mental health, youth development, and social stability.

contributions.claim: Argues that rapid feedback loops and on-the-fly personalization could produce unprecedented compulsive consumption when combined with engagement-maximizing incentives.
Connects tailored real-time generation with possible autonomy erosion, emotional distress, and disproportionate risks for vulnerable groups, particularly adolescents.
Calls for strong government oversight, design guidelines, public-health collaboration, and targeted measures for responsible deployment.

stated_novelty.claim: The paper presents real-time hyper-personalized generative AI as a potential new category of addictive digital media, termed “digital heroin,” and extends the regulatory concern to generative content generation.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report drawing on clinical observations of social-media addiction and neuroscientific research on dopamine-driven feedback to illustrate risks from real-time tailored content.
The authors report that real-time generation may erode autonomy, cause emotional distress, and disproportionately endanger adolescents and other vulnerable groups.
The authors report that shortening generation feedback to seconds enables on-the-fly hyper-personalization, which could intensify compulsive consumption under engagement-driven incentives.

narrative_sequence.summary: Real-time generative AI is framed as a possible next wave of addictive digital media with serious mental-health and youth-development implications.
Seconds-level generation feedback is presented as enabling on-the-fly hyper-personalization.
Engagement-maximizing incentives are linked to possible compulsive consumption and wider cognitive, social, and mental-health consequences.
The paper calls for substance-like government oversight, especially for minors, alongside proactive technical and public-health measures.

source_observation.claim: The abstract links a technical capability, an incentive structure, specific harms, and affected populations before making regulatory recommendations.

lessons.interpretation: This creates a traceable bridge from system design to policy claims.
lessons.application: When presenting governance proposals, explicitly map the enabling capability and incentive to concrete harms and named vulnerable groups before stating the intervention.
lessons.exception: This framing is unsuitable when the system lacks a plausible mechanism connecting its capability or incentives to the proposed harm.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify empirical study designs, quantitative effect sizes, or causal evidence for the predicted addiction-like effects.
The scope and operational details of the proposed oversight, design guidelines, and targeted policy measures are not given.
The abstract does not state a limitation in prior approaches or a comparison establishing priority over existing work.
